review_basis: Visually inspected every original numbered WebP in this part. Narration follows the exact visual reading order, shown AWS components, sample values and distinctions. All slides 24–36 visually checked as a complete consecutive section.
part_title: SageMaker Build, Operate and DeepAR Review

scenes.title: SageMaker – Summary: Build
scenes.narration: This summary connects the tools needed to prepare and build an ML model. Across the top, Data Wrangler prepares and transforms raw records. Feature Store shares reusable feature definitions and values across teams. Ground Truth is illustrated as a human labeling workflow; the slide explicitly notes availability for existing customers only. Automatic Model Tuning tests different hyperparameter settings to improve a validation metric. SageMaker Clarify assesses potential bias and provides explanations of model behavior. The customer churn example below follows that same broad teaching order: clean customer usage and support records, maintain shared features, label historical churn outcomes, tune a predictive model and inspect whether results differ across customer segments. This is a service-selection comparison, not a claim that every project must use all five tools or in exactly this sequence. The exam cue is to match the requirement to the service: prepare, reuse, label, tune, or analyze fairness and explainability. Human review and separate evaluation remain essential, even when automation is available.

scenes.title: SageMaker – Summary: Operate
scenes.narration: This slide contrasts five concerns after a model is created. First choose an inference mode: real-time for fast interactive requests, serverless for intermittent traffic, asynchronous for long individual jobs, or Batch Transform for large offline datasets. Second, monitor production data and prediction quality to detect issues or drift. Third, retain model metadata and evaluation evidence for transparency. Fourth, Model Registry manages version histories and approvals. Fifth, SageMaker Pipelines coordinates the repeatable workflow. The bottom example puts those services together. When a drift alert appears, the operator investigates the data, executes a configured pipeline to retrain and evaluate, registers the new version with supporting evidence, approves it, deploys it, then updates the model card. The arrows do not mean an alert should always force retraining: a human or policy gate should confirm the cause and evaluate the new model first. The exam decision cue asks you to select the inference mode according to latency and workload, while the other services handle monitoring, documentation, approvals and orchestration.

scenes.title: SageMaker – Extra Features
scenes.narration: The top architecture explains network isolation for a SageMaker training job. Input training data lives in Amazon S3 on the left. SageMaker supplies it through a managed data channel to the training container, shown inside a dashed isolation boundary with a padlock. When network isolation is enabled, the training container cannot freely contact the internet or other networks, but SageMaker can still arrange managed input delivery and write model artifacts back to S3 on the right. The bottom retail example then introduces DeepAR, a probabilistic forecasting algorithm trained on related time series such as product demand at multiple stores. Look carefully at the plot: historical demand is a yellow fluctuating line, the dashed cyan future line is a median forecast, and the purple shaded region represents a range of plausible future demand values, labeled as an example 80 percent prediction interval. Probabilistic forecasting expresses uncertainty rather than claiming one exact future outcome. The two concepts on this slide are distinct exam cues: network isolation limits container network access, and DeepAR models distributions of future values for related time series.
